title: Arctic Tale
full_review:
"Arctic Tale" (Paramount Classics) is an absorbing story charting the parallel journeys of Nanu, a polar bear cub, and Seela, a walrus pup, in the Arctic Circle, from birth to maturity. It shows how they manage to survive a changing environment with ever-decreasing ice seriously impeding both their natural habitat and their ability to obtain food.

These are new challenges never before encountered by these species, we are informed in the film's eco-friendly narration, thanks to Linda Woolverton, Mose Richards and Kristin Gore's whimsical script.

The scenes of young Nanu and Seela being nurtured by their mothers -- and in the case of Seela, by another walrus referred to as Auntie, who takes Seela under her wing -- are extraordinary. (Auntie will eventually make the ultimate sacrifice when the walrus herd is attacked by a big bear.)

Other highlights include Nanu's mother teaching Nanu how to hunt walruses, and later, permanently driving Nanu away from her when she cannot care for both of them. This scene, like all the others, is given a highly anthropomorphized spin, but on the whole, you willingly succumb to the storytelling.

The close-ups of the walruses are a particular revelation, as we see what a close-knit community they are, and how they care for their young, memorizing each other's faces with their whiskers.

How much of this so-called "fable" can be chalked up to dramatic license is difficult to determine, but events play out plausibly.

An inspired choice as narrator, Queen Latifah strikes just the right tone: both knowledgeable and accessible.

Co-directors and cinematographers Adam Ravetch and Sarah Robertson (husband and wife) have fashioned an impressively photographed National Geographic production (with Visionbox Films). The challenges facing these creatures in light of global warming render the film a vivid animal counterpart to "An Inconvenient Truth," written by Kristin Gore's dad, Al.

The admirable environmental message -- by 2040, the film asserts, the summer sea ice could be almost completely gone -- is clear enough without a somewhat cloying credit sequence at the end, with children telling us such factoids that if we turn off a light bulb we'll be saving the planet. But the film itself is a winner.

Though restrained in its presentation, the film includes some images of animal violence and death, perhaps precluding viewing by the very young. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences. All ages admitted.
